newsitem.title: ITALY: FAO says 96 cereal output bigger than expected.
newsitem.headline: FAO says 96 cereal output bigger than expected.

text.p: The U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) said world cereal production in 1996 was bigger than previously thought and that the forecast for this year looked satisfactory.
FAO said both these positive signs meant an improvement in the outlook for global food supplies, although carryover stocks were expected nevertheless to remain below minimum safe levels.
The agency said in its January-February Food Outlook that 1996 world cereal production was estimated at 1.872 billion tonnes, about 23 million tonnes more than its last forecast.

It said the increase reflected larger than expected wheat production in South America and Australia, where harvests have just been completed, and an upward adjustment in the final estimate of U.S. coarse grain crops.

FAO's estimate for 1996 world wheat production was estimated to increase 7.5 percent over 1995 at 588 million tonnes, coarse grains was up 11.6 percent over previous year to 905 million tonnes and rice was up 2.2 percent to 379 million tonnes.

"This level of production is expected to lead to increased utilisation of cereals in 1996-97 and to a substantial replenishment of aggregate carryover stocks for the first time in four years," the outlook said.

It said that despite the increase in stocks, the ratio of end-of-season stocks to trend utilisation in 1997-98, now estimated at close to 16 percent, would still be below the 17-18 percent range that FAO considers the minimum necessary to safeguard world food security.
"Thus, global food security in the coming 1997-98 season will once again depend on another good cereal crop in 1997."
FAO said early prospects for 1997 wheat crops looked "mostly satisfactory".

It said that in the United States, despite a seven percent reduction in plantings, favourable conditions so far point to less winterkill this year, and the harvested area might turn out to be similar to that in 1996.

The report said a bumper wheat crop was expected in China and above average crops in India and Pakistan. It added that winter wheat plantings also were reported to be up again in the major European producers.
The outlook said world trade in cereals in 1996-97 is now forecast at 186 million tonnes, 20 million tonnes less than shipments in the previous year.
It said the decrease in trade was due to lower imports of wheat and coarse grains.
